title: Cyber Defenders Unit 2 · Keys and secret codes (3-5)

items.q: Which of these passphrases is the strongest?
choices: cat, because it is short and easy to type
purple volcano teapot giraffe, because four random words make it long and hard to guess
birthday123, because numbers always make it safe
my best friend's name, because it feels personal
items.why: A guessing computer tries short words and birthdays first, and a word with numbers stuck on is only a little longer. Every extra random word multiplies the guesses it needs.

choices: Your best friend, if they promise not to tell
Your teammates, so they can play as you
Only you and a trusted adult
Anyone online who asks for it nicely
items.why: Your passphrase is what proves the mailbox is yours. Anyone who knows it can open it as you, so only you and the adult who helps look after your account may know it.

items.q: Your best friend asks for your passphrase so they can play as you. What should you do?
choices: Say no and keep it secret, and tell a trusted adult if they keep asking
Share it, because best friends share everything
Share half of it, so it stays a bit secret
Share it just once, then forget about it
items.why: With your passphrase, your friend could say things as you, and you could not prove it was not you. A real friend can play with their own account.

items.q: Sam's mailbox holds Sam's private letters. Who should be able to open it?
choices: Anyone who finds the key on the road
Sam and the trusted adult who helps Sam
Any visitor who is curious about the letters
A friend who wants to borrow Sam's account
items.why: Private letters belong to their owner. A found key or a curious visitor does not earn a look.

items.q: Why does a second lock help if a mailbox key is lost?
choices: The finder still needs the second step sent to a phone at home, so the key alone is not enough
It makes the lost key grow longer and stronger
It lets anyone open the mailbox without a key
It makes a spare copy of all the letters inside
items.why: Two different steps guard the box. The lost key alone cannot open it without the code sent home.

items.q: Which one is a spare copy of your things, kept somewhere else?
choices: A passphrase
A second lock
A cipher
A backup
items.why: A backup is the spare copy kept somewhere else, ready for the day the first copy is lost.

items.q: A code shifts each plain letter forward by 3 to make the secret word FDW. What plain word does FDW say?
choices: PIG
HEN
CAT
FOX
items.why: Shift each letter of FDW back by 3: F to C, D to A, W to T. The plain word is CAT.

items.q: In a cipher, what is the key?
choices: The secret setting, like shift by 3, that you need to read the code
The envelope the message travels in
The road the message takes to a friend
The funny picture that helps you remember words
items.why: The key is the secret setting of the cipher. Without it, the scrambled letters stay scrambled.

items.q: Why does scrambling protect a message traveling on an open road?
choices: Nobody carrying it can see the message at all
Anyone who peeks sees only mixed-up letters they cannot read without the key
The message travels much faster than plain letters
The letters turn into pictures that only owls can read
items.why: Scrambling turns the words into mixed-up letters. A peeker without the key cannot read them.
